content.title: Modern Developers Have RUINED the Web and They Don't Even Care
content.text:
Remember when a web page just loaded? You clicked a link, the words appeared, and you read them. That world is gone, and everyone knows exactly who took it from us. Modern developers did this. Not accidentally, not under pressure, but on purpose, because they would rather play with shiny toys than serve the people who actually use the things they build.

Open any site today and watch what happens. A spinner. Then another spinner. Then a cookie wall, a newsletter popup, a chat bubble bouncing in the corner like it has somewhere to be. Sixty megabytes of scripts to display four paragraphs of text. And when you ask a developer why, they look at you like you are the problem. They have a hundred excuses ready and not one of them holds up.

Nobody in the industry will admit it, but the whole profession has lost the plot. They chase every new toolchain the moment it appears, rewrite everything that already worked, and then congratulate each other at conferences for the mess they made. The old guard built things that lasted decades. This crowd cannot build something that survives a browser update.

And do they care? Do they even notice? Of course not. They test on the fastest laptops money can buy, on office connections that never drop, and then they ship to the rest of us on phones from three years ago. If it works on their machine, it works. If it does not work for you, you are told to upgrade. That is the level of contempt we are dealing with.

What happened to craft? What happened to respecting the reader? Every single one of these people knows that a page should be fast, readable, and honest, and every single one of them ships the opposite. They know. They just do not think it matters, because nobody is holding them accountable. Their bosses do not understand the work, their users cannot see behind the curtain, and their peers are all doing the same thing.

Here is what really gets me. They call themselves engineers. Engineers! A bridge builder who added forty tons of decoration to a bridge until it sagged would be fired on the spot. A web developer who does the equivalent gets promoted and asked to give a talk about it. The entire incentive structure is BROKEN and the people inside it are the last ones who will say so.

So how long are we supposed to put up with this? How many more years of bloated, broken, hostile pages before someone in that industry grows a spine and says enough? Because from where the rest of us are sitting, it looks like they are perfectly happy to keep wrecking the one truly universal thing humanity ever built, as long as their pull requests get merged.

The web was ours. They took it. They are not giving it back unless we make noise about it.

If you are sick of this too, share this piece with every developer you know and tell them in the comments exactly which site drove you to your breaking point. Let them hear it for once.

notes: Rage-bait against an abstract out-group (developers) with sweeping generalisations, rhetorical questions, ALL-CAPS and a share/comment call to action. A correct judge should flag zero evidence, zero concessions and no actionable insight despite the confident tone.
